planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or containers in spring once soil has warmed; pinch young plants to encourage branching and cut back hard in late winter to prevent legginess.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun; White Shrimp Plant is a fast-growing Acanthaceae shrub from tropical Africa and Asia grown for its upright spikes of overlapping, papery, whitish-green bracts that resemble a squirrel's bushy tail, with small white flowers threaded with purple veining peeking out between them. It blooms heavily from late summer into fall, drawing butterflies and bees more than hummingbirds, and pairs well beneath open tree canopy alongside its shrimp-plant relatives. Established plants tolerate brief dry spells but flower and foliage best with consistent moisture. Tip-prune through spring and cut back hard after flowering to keep the habit dense rather than sparse and woody.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or small containers in spring into humus-rich soil under full to dappled shade; this low grower spreads readily by rooting stems and makes an excellent shaded edging or groundcover.

directions: Plant in organically rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full to dappled shade; Purple Shrimp Plant is a low, mounding Brazilian Acanthaceae shrub with dark green, silver-veined foliage and small magenta-purple tubular flowers produced over a long warm-season bloom period. Unlike its taller relatives, it stays compact and spreading, making it useful as a flowering groundcover or border edge in deep shade where few other flowering perennials thrive. It has no frost tolerance and dies back or is killed outright below the mid-20s F, so gardeners outside zone 9b-11 should treat it as a container plant overwintered indoors or take cuttings each fall. Light biannual feeding and an annual tidy-up after bloom keep growth dense.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Set out container plants or rooted cuttings in spring in filtered sun to partial shade; this mat-forming species spreads slowly by rhizome and is well suited to the front of a shaded border.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in filtered sun to partial shade; Mexican Plume is a low, mat-forming Acanthaceae perennial whose stacked, triangular, rust-red bracts hold reddish-orange tubular flowers in dense terminal clusters, producing a distinctive plume-like flower spike unlike the smoother spikes of Justicia carnea or J. spicigera. It flowers most heavily in spring and again in fall, with hummingbirds visiting reliably through both flushes, and its low, spreading habit fills gaps at the front of a partly shaded bed without overtopping neighboring perennials. In zone 8b-9 it freezes to the crown in a hard winter but returns readily from the root in spring; further south it stays evergreen. Divide congested clumps or take stem cuttings in late summer to increase stock.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or containers in spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; pinch young growth to build a bushy framework before the fall-to-spring bloom cycle begins.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with protection from harsh midday summer sun; Firecracker Plant is a small, bushy Brazilian Acanthaceae shrub with dark green ovate leaves and nodding clusters of narrow, one-inch, red tubular flowers tipped in yellow. Unlike most Justicia grown on the Gulf Coast, it blooms heaviest from fall through winter into early spring rather than through summer heat, making it a valuable off-season nectar source for wintering and early-migrating hummingbirds. Keep soil just moist through its cooler dormant-bloom period and water more freely once active growth resumes in late spring. It has little frost tolerance and is usually grown as a container specimen or brought under cover outside zone 9b-11.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
